name: Boron
kicker: Element 5 · The metalloid behind borax, slime, and heat-resistant glass
briefing: Boron is element number five, a hard, dark metalloid that is never found pure in nature. Its best-known mineral, borax, is used in laundry boosters and is the secret ingredient that turns white glue into stretchy homemade slime. Boron also helps make the heat-resistant glass used in lab beakers, and it keeps nuclear reactors under control by soaking up stray neutrons.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: William Lipscomb won the 1976 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for explaining how compounds of this element and hydrogen are held together by three-center, two-electron bonds. In the simplest of those compounds, two hydrogen atoms form bridges between two atoms of this element.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 5, found in the mineral borax.

tossups.p: Herbert C. Brown shared the 1979 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for using compounds of this element in organic reactions, such as a two-step reaction that adds water across a double bond. Akira Suzuki’s coupling reaction joins carbon atoms using organic compounds of this element and palladium.
tossups.r: This element’s best-known mineral is borax. For 10 points, name this metalloid with atomic number 5.

tossups.p: This element is made mostly when cosmic rays smash larger atomic nuclei in space, rather than by fusion inside stars, which helps explain why it is rare in the universe. Its two stable isotopes have mass numbers 10 and 11.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element, the lightest in group 13, which sits just left of carbon on the periodic table.

tossups.p: This element’s isotope with mass number 10 absorbs neutrons so well that the element is used in control rods and dissolved in the cooling water of some nuclear reactors to keep the chain reaction in check.
tossups.r: This element’s carbide is one of the hardest materials known and is used in armor. For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 5.

tossups.p: Adding a tiny amount of this element to silicon creates “holes” and makes a p-type semiconductor, because each of its atoms has one fewer valence electron than a silicon atom. It is the only metalloid in group 13.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element, whose mineral borax is used in laundry products and homemade slime.

tossups.p: This element’s trifluoride is a classic Lewis acid: its central atom has only six electrons around it, so it eagerly accepts a pair of electrons from ammonia. That flat, triangular molecule is a famous exception to the octet rule.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element with three valence electrons, the first member of group 13.

tossups.p: The strongest permanent magnets, used in headphones and electric car motors, are made of neodymium, iron, and this element. This element is also a micronutrient that plants need to build strong cell walls.
tossups.r: This element is a metalloid at the top of group 13. For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 5, found in borax.

tossups.p: In the 1880s, teams of twenty mules hauled wagons full of a mineral of this element out of Death Valley, California. One of the world’s largest mines for that mineral is near a California town named after this element.
tossups.r: That mineral, borax, is used in cleaning products. For 10 points, name this metalloid with atomic number 5.

tossups.p: The mineral ulexite [“YOO-lek-site”], a source of this element, is nicknamed “TV rock” because its bundled fibers carry an image from one side of the stone to the other. Turkey holds most of the world’s reserves of this element’s minerals.
tossups.r: This metalloid has atomic number 5. For 10 points, name this element found in borax and boric acid.

tossups.p: Ions containing this element and oxygen link the long molecules in white glue together, turning the glue into stretchy homemade slime. An acid of this element mixed with silicone oil produced the bouncy toy Silly Putty.
tossups.r: This element has atomic number 5. For 10 points, name this element found in the cleaning powder borax.

tossups.p: Compounds of this element give a bright green color to flames; for example, a solution of its acid in methanol burns green. That acid is also a mild antiseptic and a common insect killer used against cockroaches.
tossups.r: That acid is boric acid. For 10 points, name this metalloid with atomic number 5.

tossups.p: In 1808, Humphry Davy in London and the team of Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac and Louis Jacques Thénard [“tay-NAR”] in Paris separately isolated this element from its acid. It sits between beryllium and carbon in the second row of the periodic table.
tossups.r: This element’s name comes from the mineral borax. For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 5.

tossups.p: Pure forms of this element are built from clusters of twelve atoms arranged in a 20-sided shape called an icosahedron [“eye-koh-suh-HEE-drun”]. This element’s nitride can form a soft, slippery solid nicknamed “white graphite” or a cubic form nearly as hard as diamond.
tossups.r: Slime recipes often use borax, a mineral of this element. For 10 points, name this metalloid, the first element in group 13.

tossups.p: Otto Schott developed a heat-resistant glass containing this element in the late 1800s, and that kind of glass is used for lab beakers because it barely expands when heated. Strong, light fibers of this element are used to stiffen aircraft parts and some sports gear.
tossups.r: This element is never found pure in nature. For 10 points, name this metalloid with atomic number 5, found in borax.

tossups.p: Kernite, a mineral named for Kern County, California, is a major ore of this element. This element’s ground-state electron configuration is 1s² 2s² 2p¹, and its average atomic mass is about 10.8.
tossups.r: Like aluminum below it, this element has three valence electrons. For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 5.

trap.title: Element, not borax
trap.body: Many clues about this element are really about its compounds: borax in slime and laundry boosters, boric acid as a cockroach killer, and the twenty-mule teams of Death Valley. Players who blurt “borax” or “boric acid” lose the points, because the question wants the element. Look-alike names are traps too: bromine, barium, and beryllium all start with B, and so does boson, a word from physics.
trap.fix: Atomic number 5, group 13, three valence electrons, “metalloid,” and neutron-absorbing control rods all mean boron (symbol B). Bromine is Br, barium is Ba, and beryllium is Be.
